Mash-up: the most popular tubal ligation is the Pomeroy technique; options are numeric codes from pasted contraception items, so none answers the stem.
PALM causes are structural, diagnosable by imaging (ultrasound) and confirmed histologically: I, II and III, which only option A expresses. Key C includes a nonexistent statement 4.
Mash-up: uterine prolapse in early pregnancy is managed with a vaginal pessary; options are numeric codes from pasted items, so none answers the stem.
Dermoid cyst is a germ cell tumour, bilateral in about 10-20%, and commonly undergoes torsion; rupture is uncommon. So I, II and III (A).
Mash-up: salpingectomy reduces epithelial ovarian cancer risk, but options are numeric codes for a pasted cervical-screening list; no option answers the stem.
Nulliparity is a risk factor and multiparity protective; late menopause, hypertension and obesity increase endometrial cancer risk.
HSG shows tubal patency after tuboplasty, synechiae and IUD position; a subserosal fibroid does not alter the cavity. I, II and III (A); stem even states Ans (a).
Mash-up: cold-knife conisation is indicated for inconsistent colposcopy, cytology and biopsy findings, but options are codes for the pasted hyperprolactinaemia list; none answers the stem.
Dysgerminoma: commonest malignant ovarian germ cell tumour, bilateral in 10-15%, highly radio- and chemosensitive (III false), fertility-sparing surgery possible; hence I, II and IV.
Preterm birth complications are the leading cause of neonatal death in India, ahead of intrapartum asphyxia, sepsis and congenital anomalies.
Raised ICP: head end 30° and midline, brief hyperventilation to PaCO2 30–35 mmHg, mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg; hypertonic, not hypotonic, saline is used.
A scatter diagram plots paired values of two variables and displays their correlation; histogram, bar and pie charts show distributions or proportions.
Bartter (NKCC2, TAL) has hypercalciuria; Gitelman (NCC, DCT) has hypocalciuria, so statement 2 is false; both are normotensive with high renin and aldosterone.
Fanconi syndrome causes proximal (type 2) RTA from bicarbonate wasting, i.e. metabolic acidosis, alongside glycosuria, phosphaturia and aminoaciduria.
Loop diuretics cause hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis; the other three pairs (loop hypercalciuria, thiazide hyponatraemia/hypocalciuria, hyperuricaemia/hypercalcaemia) are correct.
Nephronophthisis is autosomal recessive; MCKD types 1 (MUC1) and 2 (UMOD) and juvenile hyperuricaemic nephropathy are autosomal dominant. Option D carries a stray heading.
Anti-GBM disease targets the alpha3 chain of type IV collagen, causes RPGN, is Goodpasture's when lungs involved; it affects young and elderly, often renal-limited in elderly.
WT1 mutations give FSGS with genital anomalies and Wilms' tumour; INF2 links to Charcot-Marie-Tooth, LMX1B to nail-patella syndrome, APOL1 is not linked to hepatic fibrosis.
Male sex, persistent heavy proteinuria, raised creatinine at presentation and tubulo-interstitial fibrosis on biopsy are all recognised poor prognostic features in glomerular disease.
Biopsy suits nephritic presentation with normal kidneys and transplant dysfunction; small kidneys (<60% predicted) and uncontrolled hypertension are contraindications. Option D has stray heading.

RBC casts-glomerulonephritis/vasculitis, WBC casts-interstitial nephritis/pyelonephritis, pigmented casts-myoglobin/haemoglobin, eosinophiluria-allergic interstitial nephritis/atheroemboli: all correctly matched.
CKD and diabetes are CIN risk factors, isotonic saline hydration is the key prevention, metformin is withheld 48 h; N-acetylcysteine cannot reverse established injury.
Schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin and reticulocytosis occur in both TMAs; severely reduced ADAMTS-13 activity (<10%) is specific to TTP.
CKD anaemia results from EPO deficiency, uraemic marrow suppression, reduced red cell survival and impaired iron intake/absorption/utilisation (hepcidin); all four contribute.
Forearm AVF created months ahead, arterialises over 4-6 weeks; upper-limb veins are preferred over leg veins; HBV-positive patients need dedicated, segregated dialysis machines.
Active uncontrolled infection is an absolute contraindication to transplantation; a negative crossmatch is required and cured cancer after a suitable interval is acceptable. Option D garbled.
Collecting duct is where ADH and aldosterone regulate water and sodium; ascending limb is water-impermeable, descending limb lacks active Na transport, PCT reabsorbs bulk bicarbonate.
Macula densa cells sense distal tubular NaCl delivery and adjust afferent arteriolar tone, mediating tubuloglomerular feedback.
Hyaline casts (with FENa <1%) indicate pre-renal azotaemia; muddy-brown granular and tubular epithelial casts and FENa >2% indicate ATN. Option D carries pasted answer text.
Contrast-induced nephropathy is an acute decline in renal function within about 48 hours of iodinated contrast, excluding other causes.
Volume expansion with isotonic saline is the most effective proven prevention for contrast nephropathy; prophylactic dialysis, steroids and diuretics do not help.
Metformin is withheld because contrast-induced AKI reduces its renal clearance and can precipitate lactic acidosis.
Gadolinium-associated nephrogenic systemic fibrosis occurs chiefly with eGFR below 30 mL/min, especially in dialysis-dependent CKD or AKI.
With severe renal impairment, use non-contrast alternatives (ultrasound, non-contrast CT/MRI) where possible; gadolinium risks nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. Option D carries stray text.
Polyuria occurs in diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus and hypokalaemic Conn's syndrome; hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia, not polyuria (hypercalcaemia does).
Primary polydipsia gives low or low-normal serum sodium with dilute urine; DI tends to high-normal sodium. Option D has explanation text merged into it.

All four statements true: diabetic osmotic diuresis, hypercalcaemia and hypokalaemia cause nephrogenic DI, primary polydipsia gives dilute urine; stem also contains a pasted oliguria question with its answer.
Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria >3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia; RBC casts and hypertension suggest nephritic. Option D contains merged explanation text.
MPGN lowers C3 via complement activation; minimal change disease, FSGS and IgA nephropathy usually have normal complement levels.
Primary nephrotic syndrome has low albumin, high LDL and heavy proteinuria, but complement is normal (minimal change, FSGS, membranous).
Membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis among nephrotic glomerulopathies (hypercoagulable state).
ISN/RPS class V lupus nephritis is membranous lupus nephritis; the other pairs are mismatched.
Oval fat bodies/fatty casts (lipiduria) characterise nephrotic syndrome; RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs indicate nephritic glomerular bleeding; WBC casts suggest pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis.
Complement is normal in most primary nephrotic syndromes (low only in some secondary causes, e.g., lupus, MPGN), so 'always low' is false. Option D carries appended text.
Stem is pasted notes on anti-GBM disease, Alport syndrome and hereditary FSGS with no numbered statements, so the option combinations cannot be evaluated.
Goodpasture antigen (NC1 domain of alpha-3 type IV collagen) is targeted in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, causing RPGN with pulmonary haemorrhage.
Anti-GBM disease is treated with plasma exchange plus corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide to remove circulating antibody and suppress its production.
Goodpasture syndrome is anti-GBM-mediated rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with pulmonary (alveolar) haemorrhage.
NKCC2 (SLC12A1) loss-of-function causes Bartter syndrome type 1: salt wasting, hypokalaemic alkalosis, hypercalciuria; Gitelman (NCC defect) gives hypocalciuria.
Gitelman syndrome (thiazide-sensitive NCC defect) features hypomagnesaemia with hypocalciuria, unlike the hypercalciuria of Bartter syndrome.
WT1 causes Wilms tumour with genital anomalies (WAGR/Denys-Drash); LMX1B is nail-patella, INF2 is FSGS with Charcot-Marie-Tooth, COL4A5 is Alport.
Alport: X-linked COL4A5 type IV collagen defect affecting kidney, cochlea and eye, presenting with haematuria; nephrotic syndrome at onset is unusual. Stem has unrelated pasted notes.
Cholesterol atheroembolism causes renal impairment, eosinophilia and livedo reticularis, typically days to weeks after angiography, not immediate collapse within minutes.
Cholesterol atheroembolic renal disease has no specific therapy; management is supportive (statins, BP control, avoiding further vascular procedures and anticoagulation).
Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis follows gadolinium-based MRI contrast exposure in patients with advanced CKD or on dialysis.
Microalbuminuria (urine albumin/ACR) is the earliest clinical marker of diabetic nephropathy, preceding any rise in creatinine or urea.
Diabetic nephropathy is the commonest cause of CKD and end-stage renal disease worldwide.
Natural history: microalbuminuria progresses to overt proteinuria, then declining GFR and end-stage renal failure.
Serum creatinine rises only after substantial nephron loss, so it is least useful for earliest detection; albumin testing detects microalbuminuria.
Albumin-specific dipsticks detect microalbuminuria below the threshold of standard protein dipsticks; quantitative ACR confirms it.
Corticosteroids have no role in diabetic nephropathy (treated with glycaemic/BP control, RAAS blockade, SGLT2i); other statements are true. Option D has appended text.
RBC casts occur in malignant hypertension and WBC casts in pyelonephritis; pigmented casts indicate myoglobin/haemoglobin, not vasculitis; granular casts typify ATN. Pair 4 debatable.
Hyaline casts (Tamm-Horsfall protein) with bland sediment typify prerenal azotemia; epithelial and muddy brown casts suggest ATN.
FENa >1% reflects impaired tubular sodium reabsorption, i.e., intrinsic (ATN) AKI; prerenal AKI has FENa <1%.
Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes) indicate glomerular origin of haematuria.
Adynamic bone disease is low-turnover renal osteodystrophy with low PTH (oversuppression by calcium/vitamin D); osteitis fibrosa cystica reflects high PTH.
Uncontrolled hypertension (like bleeding diathesis or small kidneys) contraindicates percutaneous renal biopsy; the other options are indications.
Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of CKD worldwide, followed by hypertension.
CKD is irreversible, with anaemia, raised PTH and small kidneys; recovery to baseline within days suggests AKI.
Calciphylaxis (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy) occurs almost exclusively in advanced CKD and dialysis patients.
Calciphylaxis begins with livedo reticularis/painful violaceous mottling, progressing to necrotic eschars and ulcers.
Calciphylaxis is also termed calcific uraemic arteriolopathy.
Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of matrix Gla protein, a recognised risk factor for calciphylaxis.
Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of matrix Gla protein, a key inhibitor of vascular calcification, which predisposes to calciphylaxis.
Calciphylaxis was historically blamed on deranged calcium-phosphorus homeostasis with advanced secondary hyperparathyroidism in ESRD. It is now often seen without severe hyperparathyroidism.
Matrix Gla protein becomes active only after vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of its glutamate residues.
A native forearm AV fistula (radiocephalic, Brescia-Cimino) is the preferred access: best patency, fewest infections and thromboses. Grafts and catheters are second-line.
HBsAg-positive dialysis patients are isolated on dedicated machines because HBV is highly transmissible and survives in the environment. This is not required for HCV or HIV.
Haemodiafiltration adds convective clearance (high-volume ultrafiltration with replacement fluid) to diffusion, which improves removal of middle molecules such as beta2-microglobulin.
During AVF maturation, arterial pressure and flow dilate the vein and thicken its wall (arterialisation) over about 4-6 weeks before it can be cannulated.
Subclavian cannulation is avoided because it causes central venous stenosis that ruins future ipsilateral access. AVF first, PTFE graft second and HBV segregation are all correct.
Active malignancy is an absolute contraindication because of the immunosuppression transplantation requires. Treated cancer after a disease-free interval, older age and controlled diabetes are not.
A treated, cured malignancy after an adequate disease-free interval does not bar transplantation. Active cancer, active infection and psychosocial barriers to adherence are contraindications.
In renal transplantation the donor ureter is implanted into the recipient bladder (ureteroneocystostomy, e.g. the extravesical Lich-Gregoir technique).
Asymptomatic bacteriuria means at least 10^5 CFU/mL of one organism in urine (in women, two consecutive samples) with no urinary symptoms.
Acute pyelonephritis classically presents with fever, loin pain and renal angle tenderness. Dysuria, frequency and urgency point to cystitis instead.
Fluoroquinolones damage cartilage (arthropathy) in immature animals, so they are avoided in pregnancy and in children.
The Meares-Stamey four-glass test localises infection to the prostate. It diagnoses chronic bacterial prostatitis, which presents as recurrent UTI in men.
Short-course trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin is the empirical first choice for uncomplicated lower UTI. Fluoroquinolones are held in reserve; gentamicin is for complicated infection.
Sulphonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, so use near term risks neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia and kernicterus.
Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a gas-forming renal infection, usually E. coli, seen mostly in diabetics. Option D has an imported topic heading appended.
Higher dietary calcium lowers stone risk because it binds oxalate in the gut. Animal protein, low urine citrate and hypercalciuria all raise risk.
Persistently acid urine (pH 5.5 or lower) is the main risk factor for uric acid stones, because uric acid is poorly soluble at low pH.
Urine pH above 6.5 favours calcium phosphate stones. Uric acid stones form below pH 5.5; struvite needs urease-driven urine above pH 7.
Calcium stones make up about 75-80% of renal calculi, mostly calcium oxalate. Uric acid, struvite and cystine stones are less common.
Hyperoxaluria (primary, enteric or dietary) raises urinary calcium oxalate supersaturation, which produces calcium oxalate stones.
Calcium oxalate is the commonest renal stone. Option D and the explanation contain pasted-in text on RCC and uric acid nephropathy.
Radical nephrectomy with en bloc removal of Gerota's fascia is the standard for localized RCC. Partial nephrectomy suits small tumours, not all cases.
RCC resists chemotherapy, and VEGF-targeted TKIs (sunitinib, pazopanib) are the mainstay for advanced disease. It is a tumour of adults; in children it is Wilms tumour.
Clear cell RCC (proximal tubule origin, VHL loss) is the commonest subtype, about 75-85%. Option D has a section heading appended.
Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which cuts uric acid production and so the urate load reaching the kidney. It does not dissolve crystals.
Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase given IV. It converts uric acid to soluble allantoin to prevent or treat tumour lysis syndrome.
Preserved nocturnal/morning erections show intact neurovascular function, pointing to psychogenic ED; gradual progression and peripheral vascular disease suggest organic causes.
Oral PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) are first-line for erectile dysfunction unless nitrate use or another contraindication is present.
Absent nocturnal erections point to organic ED. Situational variability, sudden onset after stress and preserved sleep erections suggest psychogenic ED. Option D has junk import text appended.
INF2: FSGS with Charcot-Marie-Tooth. LMX1B: nail-patella syndrome. WT1: Denys-Drash/Frasier/WAGR (genital anomalies, Wilms tumour, intellectual disability).
Liddle syndrome is autosomal dominant ENaC gain of function, with hypertension and hypokalaemic alkalosis. Renin and aldosterone are suppressed, so statement 3 is false.
MCKD1 (MUC1) and familial juvenile hyperuricaemic nephropathy (UMOD) are autosomal dominant. Nephronophthisis is autosomal recessive. All three pairs are correct.
Loop diuretics block NKCC2 and abolish the lumen-positive potential, causing hypercalciuria. Thiazides cause hypocalciuria, hyperuricaemia and metabolic alkalosis.
RBC casts (GN/vasculitis), WBC casts (pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis) and RTE casts (ATN) are correct. Lipid casts mean nephrotic syndrome; pre-renal sediment is bland or hyaline.
Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes) on phase-contrast microscopy show the haematuria is glomerular.
Pre-renal: FENa <1%, urine osmolality >500, low urine Na. Options A, C, D describe ATN. Option B lost its '<1%' text; option D carries the explanation.
A solitary native kidney is a relative contraindication to percutaneous renal biopsy, not an indication. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct.

Active infection and active malignancy absolutely contraindicate renal transplant. Treated cancer with long remission, controlled hypertension and resolved HBV do not. Option D carries the explanation text.
Dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut, lowering oxaluria and stone risk. High sodium and animal protein raise risk; citrate inhibits crystallisation.
JME usually relapses when AEDs are stopped and needs lifelong valproate or levetiracetam. Benign neonatal, febrile and Rolandic seizures are self-limiting.
Standard texts link the migraine headache phase to extracranial vasodilatation (a dated vascular view). Common migraine is migraine without aura; aura is most often visual.
Sleep deprivation, missed AED doses, recreational drug misuse and physical or mental exhaustion are all recognised seizure triggers.
Hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency and thiamine deficiency are treatable causes of dementia. Dementia with Lewy bodies is progressive and neurodegenerative.
4AT items: Alertness, AMT4, Attention (months backwards), Acute change or fluctuating course. Apnoea is not one of them.
Brain death needs irreversible unresponsive coma, absent brainstem reflexes and apnoea despite raised PaCO2. Hypothermia must be excluded first; it is not a criterion.
Alzheimer's is a cortical dementia affecting short- and long-term memory, so statement II is false. Anosognosia (denial) and depression are common.
Flickering lights, recreational drug misuse, AED non-compliance and sleep deprivation are all recognised seizure triggers.
Familial Alzheimer's (APP/presenilin), Huntington's and Wilson's disease are inherited. Punch-drunk syndrome is traumatic, and only option A leaves it out.
Recent head injury, recent MI and GI bleeding within 21 days contraindicate rtPA. The BP cut-off is >185/110, so >150/100 is not a contraindication.
Atypical antipsychotics (dopamine blockade), lithium and the nigral toxin MPTP all produce drug- or toxin-induced parkinsonism.
Sickle cell disease, smoking and atrial fibrillation raise stroke risk. High fibrinogen, not hypofibrinogenaemia, is the risk factor.
HIV, alcohol and phenytoin cause polyneuropathy. Among TB drugs, isoniazid causes neuropathy; rifampicin does not.
A dominant parietal lesion gives dysphasia, acalculia and dyslexia (Gerstmann features). Contralateral neglect is a sign of the non-dominant parietal lobe.
Cutaneous schwannomas belong to NF2; NF1 has axillary freckling and neurofibromas. Only B excludes schwannomas, though angiomas are not a classic NF1 feature.
The occipital pole (macular cortex) gets a dual supply from PCA and MCA collaterals, so a PCA infarct spares macular vision.
Alzheimer's, Huntington's and thiamine deficiency (Wernicke-Korsakoff) cause dementia. Vitamin D toxicity causes hypercalcaemic confusion but is not a recognised dementia cause.
Hormone receptor-positive endometrial cancers carry better prognosis; grade 3, aneuploidy and HER-2/neu overexpression are poor prognostic factors.
Stem asks about carbohydrate metabolism but lists arteries; uterus is supplied by uterine, ovarian and vaginal arteries, not inferior vesical, so the intended answer is 1, 2 and 3.
Bartholin gland lies in the superficial perineal pouch, secretes alkaline mucus on arousal and is homologous to the bulbourethral gland; its duct is columnar-lined except near the orifice.
Ureter is at risk at the infundibulopelvic ligament, beside the cervix when clamping the cardinal ligament, and at the vaginal angle; not during round ligament division.
At 12 months a child stands alone, plays a simple ball game and says 1–2 meaningful words; a vocabulary of about 10 words comes at 18 months.
Frequent relapses need ≥2 relapses within 6 months of initial response or ≥4 in 12 months; 3 steroid-responsive relapses over 18 months, none on tapering, is infrequent.
Statements were imported as options and statement 4 is missing; the explanation marks 1, 2 and 4 correct, matching the code '1, 2 and 4 only' (likely B).
Stem is a pasted page mixing pasteurisation, ergonomics and other questions; options are statement codes, not tests (the intended answer, orthotoluidine test, is absent).
NACO PPTCT: infants of HIV-positive mothers receive daily nevirapine syrup from birth (6–12 weeks by risk); stavudine, indinavir and ritonavir are not used.
In young infants (<2 months) fast breathing means ≥60/min, so 50/min is not a PSBI sign; chest indrawing, low temperature and reduced movement are. Temperature text garbled.
Abacavir is a guanosine-analogue NRTI; amprenavir and indinavir are protease inhibitors and nevirapine is an NNRTI.
SAM with shock: 15 mL/kg over the first hour of Ringer lactate with 5% dextrose or N/2 saline in 5% dextrose, with close monitoring (WHO protocol).
Early-onset OA presents before 45, usually in one joint with clear prior trauma. The altered '55' makes statement 1 false by exam convention, though logically arguable.
Oligoarthritis with inflammatory back pain after urethritis, sterile cultures and synovial fluid with multinucleated macrophages (Reiter cells) means reactive arthritis.
Davidson: in older patients gout is more often secondary to diuretics/CKD and favours upper-limb joints; presentation is often atypical (tophi, chronic), not classic acute attacks.
Ureteric narrowings: pelviureteric junction, pelvic-brim crossing of iliac vessels, intramural course and orifice; the ureter does not cross the aorta.
RCC (Grawitz tumour) shows haematuria in only about half of cases; pyrexia is a paraneoplastic feature and renal-vein tumour thrombus may embolise to lungs.
RCC arises from proximal tubular epithelium, is commoner in males (2:1), main subtypes clear cell/papillary/chromophobe; nephrectomy is mainstay for localised disease.
Davidson lists occupational coal dust, silica and cadmium as COPD risk factors; asbestos causes asbestosis, pleural disease and malignancy rather than COPD.
In cABCDE the lowercase c means control of catastrophic external haemorrhage before airway; uppercase C is circulation.
Stem lost statements 2-3 (text between < and > stripped): only hypothermia, '5 mmol/L' and BP <100 remain; intended answer excludes BP <100 mmHg.
NICE: retrograde amnesia >30 minutes (with LOC/amnesia) warrants CT within 8 hours; GCS <13, post-traumatic seizure, open/depressed fracture require CT within 1 hour.
Tension pneumothorax is clinical; needle decompression (2nd ICS MCL, ATLS 10 prefers 4th/5th ICS) then chest drain 5th ICS; pericardiocentesis is for tamponade.
Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade is hypotension, distended neck veins (raised JVP) and muffled heart sounds; option A is Cushing's triad.

Traumatic tamponade needs surgical decompression/repair (clotted blood, ongoing bleeding), pericardiocentesis only temporising; small-volume tamponade is true but does not explain avoiding pericardiocentesis.
Spleen is classically the most frequently injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma (ATLS laparotomy series 40-55%); some recent texts cite liver as commonest.
eFAST detects fluid in abdomen, pleura and pericardium but needs about 100-250 mL (DPL detects ~20 mL), misses solid-organ injury without haemoperitoneum and retroperitoneum.
In blunt trauma DPL is positive with >100,000 RBC/mm3, >500 WBC/mm3, frank blood, bile, bacteria or food fibres.
Chronic subdural haematoma is a crescentic concavo-convex hypodense collection on CT; biconvex hyperdense lens is extradural, corpus callosum foci suggest DAI.
Text between < and > was stripped: ICP and sodium targets are fused ('ICP 140 mmol/L'); intended answer excludes CPP >80 mmHg (target CPP 60-70).
DAI is a pathological diagnosis; CT is often normal or only suggestive (petechial haemorrhages), while MRI is more sensitive.
ASIA C: incomplete injury with motor function preserved below the level but most key muscles below grade 3; B is sensory only, D motor grade 3 or more.
Basal skull fracture signs: otorrhoea, CSF rhinorrhoea, Battle's sign, raccoon eyes; unilateral mydriasis with ptosis indicates oculomotor compression from uncal herniation.
Flail chest is multiple adjacent ribs (classically three or more) each fractured in two or more places, producing a paradoxically moving segment.
Trauma is the commonest cause of SAH overall; ruptured berry aneurysm is commonest for spontaneous SAH. Option D carries an import artefact ('BATCH 2 — Q21 TO Q40').
Early total care requires physiological stability with lactate below 2 mmol/L (normal range); higher values favour further resuscitation or damage control.
Primary survey covers oxygenation/circulation and disability (pupils, GCS, glucose); mechanism of injury belongs to the history/secondary survey.
CRASH-2: tranexamic acid benefit is greatest within 1 hour of injury; it must start within 3 hours, later dosing may be harmful.
Glasgow Outcome Scale: 1 death, 2 vegetative state, 3 severe disability, 4 moderate disability, 5 good recovery.
Rising respiratory rate, rising pulse and falling BP indicate ongoing haemorrhage; a falling lactate signals improving perfusion.
Massive haemothorax: shock, flat neck veins, unilateral absent breath sounds and dullness; A is tension pneumothorax, C tamponade, D flail chest.
The diaphragm rises to about the fifth intercostal space in expiration, so penetrating wounds at/below it suggest diaphragmatic injury (ATLS nipple-line/fourth-space convention differs slightly).
Diaphragm injuries are often silent; NG tube on CXR shows stomach in chest; laparoscopy/VATS most accurate; penetrating injuries repaired via abdomen, so statement 4 false.
Gunshot wounds: small bowel most injured (~50%), then colon and liver; liver leads only in stab wounds.
Deceleration shears bowel at fixed-mobile junctions, classically proximal jejunum at the duodenojejunal flexure (ligament of Treitz); ileocaecal junction is the less-cited site.
Midface fractures are imaged with occipitomental views (OM ~10-15 degrees and 30 degrees); OPG and PA mandible are for mandibular fractures.
Axonotmesis: intact sheath/endoneurial tubes, axonal disruption, Wallerian degeneration; spontaneous regeneration is usual, so surgery is not mandatory.
Tscherne grades soft-tissue injury in closed fractures; Gustilo-Anderson grades open fractures; Ganga Hospital score is for severe open injuries.
Lethal six: airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest; aortic injury belongs to the hidden (potentially lethal) six.
Both statements true; dual supply explains tolerance of hepatic artery ligation but not why portal vein ligation is avoided, so A versus B is debatable.
GCS eye opening: spontaneous 4, to speech 3, to pain 2, none 1.
GCS maxima: eye 4, verbal 5, motor 6; intubated patients are scored 'T' for verbal, so only statement 3 is false.
Extradural haematoma is a biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense collection limited by sutures; subdural haematoma is crescentic.
Cushing's triad of raised ICP: hypertension (widened pulse pressure), bradycardia and irregular respiration.
Whole-body contrast CT is the gold-standard imaging for the severely injured adult blunt-trauma patient; FAST is a bedside triage adjunct.
Damage-control resuscitation uses balanced 1:1:1 packed cells:plasma:platelets to approximate whole blood and limit coagulopathy.
EDH: middle meningeal artery, squamous temporal fracture, biconvex hyperdense on CT; usually needs urgent craniotomy, so statement 4 is false.
Battle's sign (mastoid ecchymosis) is a classical sign of basal skull fracture.
In basal skull fracture blind nasogastric intubation risks intracranial passage through the cribriform plate; use the orogastric route.
Chronic subdural haematoma is hypodense on CT, so statement 3 is false; B is the only combination excluding it.
Traumatic SAH is managed conservatively; clipping/coiling apply to aneurysmal SAH and lumbar puncture is not indicated.
Neurapraxia is conduction block without axonal or sheath disruption and no Wallerian degeneration, so spontaneous recovery follows; R explains A.
Serum amylase/lipase are insensitive for pancreatic injury (statement 3 false); D is the only option excluding it.
Stab wounds injure liver most (~40%) but gunshot wounds small bowel most (~50%); texts differ on which leads in 'penetrating trauma' overall.
In paediatric blunt abdominal trauma the spleen and liver are the most frequently injured organs; kidney ranks after them.

Phytobezoars (vegetable matter) form with gastric stasis, classically after gastric surgery such as vagotomy. Trichobezoars occur in young women with trichotillomania.
GISTs are submucosal mesenchymal tumours, so mucosal biopsy is often non-diagnostic unless ulcerated. They are not epithelial, and size alone does not exclude malignancy.
Gastric outlet obstruction causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Resuscitation is isotonic (0.9%) saline with potassium supplementation.
Erosive (acute haemorrhagic) gastritis is classically NSAID-related. Autoimmune gastritis causes pernicious anaemia; Menetrier's is TGF-alpha related.
GISTs carry activating KIT (or PDGFRA) mutations. The tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib is effective for unresectable or metastatic disease.
Classic MELD uses bilirubin, INR and creatinine and excludes albumin. The newer MELD 3.0 adds albumin and sex.
Schistosomiasis causes pre-sinusoidal intrahepatic portal hypertension. Portal vein thrombosis is pre-hepatic, cirrhosis sinusoidal, Budd-Chiari post-sinusoidal.
Portal or splenic vein thrombosis is a pre-sinusoidal extrahepatic cause. Budd-Chiari and VOD are post-sinusoidal; sarcoidosis is intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal.
FNH contains Kupffer cells (it takes up sulphur colloid). Absence of Kupffer cells is characteristic of hepatic adenoma.
Budd-Chiari with relatively normal parenchyma: decompress with TIPSS or a side-to-side portocaval shunt. Transplantation is reserved for fulminant failure or cirrhosis.

Alternating strictures and dilatations of the main pancreatic duct, the 'chain of lakes', are characteristic of chronic pancreatitis.
Of the options, the appendix is the classic most common GI carcinoid site. Modern registries rank ileum and rectum higher, but neither is offered.
Right colon cancers bleed occultly, causing iron-deficiency anaemia, and present as a mass. Left-sided cancers cause altered habit, rectal bleeding and obstruction.
PSC, like ankylosing spondylitis and sacroiliitis, runs independently of IBD activity. Erythema nodosum, episcleritis and large-joint arthritis parallel activity.
Restorative proctocolectomy with IPAA removes all disease-bearing mucosa and preserves continence. It is the procedure of choice for young patients with refractory UC.
UC shows mucosal cryptitis, crypt abscesses and crypt architectural distortion. Granulomas and transmural inflammation point to Crohn's disease.
Chronic fissures (sentinel tag, hypertrophied papilla, indurated edges) lie mostly in the posterior midline in both sexes. Anterior fissures are commoner in women.
Third-degree piles need manual reduction and are not permanently prolapsed, so 1, 2 and 4 correct. Option A empty; spurious statements 5-7 (one revealing the answer) appended.
Intersphincteric fistulas are the most common type in Parks' classification, followed by trans-sphincteric.
Lymph above the dentate line drains to internal iliac nodes and below it to superficial inguinal nodes, so statement B is false.
The cystic lymph node (Lund/Mascagni) lies superficial to the cystic artery and guides its identification. The other statements describe the hepatocystic triangle correctly.
Peutz-Jeghers: autosomal dominant STK11 (19p13) mutation with mucocutaneous pigmentation. Polyps are hamartomatous, mainly in the small bowel, so statement 4 is false.
Meckel's is a true diverticulum with all bowel-wall layers and its own vitelline-derived blood supply; antimesenteric site, ~60 cm from ileocaecal valve and heterotopic mucosa are true.
Neostigmine is contraindicated with recent MI, arrhythmias, bronchial asthma and renal insufficiency; hypokalaemia is a correctable precipitant of pseudo-obstruction, not a contraindication.
Ankylosing spondylitis/sacroiliitis (and PSC) run independently of IBD activity; erythema nodosum, peripheral large-joint arthropathy and episcleritis parallel bowel disease activity.
NETs arise from Kulchitsky (enterochromaffin) cells; chromogranin A reflects tumour bulk and recurrence; they are generally resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so statement 4 is false.

Glaucomatous optic neuropathy shows enlarged cup-to-disc ratio and neuroretinal rim notching; star exudates, drusen and CNV are retinal/macular findings. Answerable without the missing image.
Middle rectal artery arises from the internal iliac, not external iliac, artery and reaches the rectum via the lateral ligaments.
Complicated pseudocysts (bleeding pseudoaneurysm, infection) are now managed first by radiological embolisation or percutaneous drainage; some texts favour surgery. Answer is source-dependent.
Synthetic absorbable meshes give minimal collagen deposition, so are unsuitable for hernia repair; used for temporary abdominal closure and buttressing suture lines.
Lockwood (low), Lotheissen (inguinal) and McEvedy (high) are femoral hernia approaches; Lytle's narrows the deep inguinal ring for indirect inguinal hernia.
Paediatric abdominal incisions are routinely closed with absorbable sutures; transverse incisions preferred not mandatory; single-layer anastomosis and subcuticular skin closure are acceptable.
Sengstaken-Blakemore balloon tamponade is a temporising measure for bleeding oesophageal/gastric varices.
Pancreatic effusion is an encapsulated pleural collection, may communicate with an abdominal collection or ascites, and requires image-guided percutaneous drainage.
Early endoscopy by an experienced endoscopist grades corrosive injury and guides management; oesophagectomy only for perforation/necrosis; lavage and blind NG insertion are contraindicated.
Hepatocystic triangle: CHD medially, inferior liver surface superiorly, cystic duct/gallbladder laterally; its key content is the cystic artery, so 1, 2, 4.
OPSI risk is highest after splenectomy for haematological disease, lowest after trauma; organisms, 2-3-year peak and vaccination 2 weeks pre-op are correct, so 1, 3, 4.
Ulcer history, sudden severe pain, rigidity, shock and free subdiaphragmatic gas indicate perforated duodenal ulcer with peritonitis.
Post-ulcer-surgery sequelae include dumping, diarrhoea, bilious vomiting and small-stomach syndrome (early satiety); increased appetite is not one.
Pyogenic liver abscess needs intravenous antibiotics plus image-guided aspiration or drainage; oral antibiotics alone are inadequate.
Multiple small fascial defects ('Swiss cheese') along a previous incision are typically found at laparoscopic ventral/incisional hernia repair.
Splenic artery aneurysm: main trunk commonest site, asymptomatic until rupture, rarely palpable (a bruit, not a thrill), so 1 and 3 only.
Valentino's syndrome: perforated peptic ulcer contents track down the right paracolic gutter, causing right iliac fossa pain mimicking appendicitis.
SBP is infection of pre-existing ascites, usually cirrhotic, without a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source.
Ogilvie's syndrome is pseudo-obstruction without mechanical cause; caecal dilatation, caecal perforation risk and IV neostigmine are correct, so 2, 3, 4.
FAP: more than 100 colorectal adenomas, usually familial, autosomal dominant APC mutation on chromosome 5q21, so 1, 2, 4.
Classical appendicitis symptoms: periumbilical colic shifting to right iliac fossa, anorexia, nausea/vomiting; constipation is not a classical feature.
Classic MELD uses bilirubin, creatinine and INR; albumin is a Child-Pugh variable (added only in MELD 3.0), so 1, 3, 4.
Typhoid ulcers lie along the gut's long axis over Peyer's patches (tubercular ulcers are transverse); perforation in third week, terminal ileum, so 1, 2, 4.
Pseudocysts are drained endoscopically, percutaneously or by surgical cystogastrostomy; pancreaticoduodenectomy is not a pseudocyst treatment, so 2, 3, 4.
